narrative_lines: He takes a small notepad from his jacket, uncaps a pen, and writes the date at the top of a clean page.
Hal: Forty years of field notes. Hard to stop.
He looks at the date he has written, then up at you.
Hal: I should say, I'm managing perfectly well. Ask anyone. Ask Dana.
He glances at the window, then back at you.
Hal: Forty years of surveys, you know. Most disputes are about where someone thinks the line is.
You offer him tea.
Hal: No tea for me. Well, only if it's brewed properly. Pot warmed first.
You bring the tea. He checks his watch against the blank wall.
Hal: Seven minutes fast, you'll notice. Ruth set it, so I'd be on time.
He does not seem to hear himself say her name.
You take a picture book from the shelf. It is called The Bear Who Followed the Map. You tell him you will read it aloud, and that he can stop you whenever something catches.
Book: Heron was leaving. Before she went, she folded a map and tucked it into Bear's paw. "Follow this," she said, "for when I am not here."
On the page, a tall grey bird stands in a doorway while a small brown paw closes around a folded paper.
Book: The first mark on the map said: Fish at dawn. So Bear fished at dawn. He set two bowls on the table, as he always had, and ate from one.
On the page, two bowls sit on a table. One is full.
Book: The next mark said: Plant beans in rows. Bear planted them in perfect rows, then stood very straight to look at them. Rabbit waved from the fence.
On the page, neat rows of beans, and a bear standing very straight.
Hal has stopped writing. The pen rests in his hand.
Hal: Sensible bear. Follows instructions. Nothing wrong with that.
Hal: Well? What's the next step?
Book: Rabbit brought a jar of jam. "Come and sit," said Rabbit. "Can't," said Bear. "I'm following the map." So Rabbit left the jam on the step.
On the page, a jar on a doorstep, and Rabbit's ears drooping.
Book: Mark after mark, day after day. Then one morning the map said: Cross the bridge. But the bridge was gone. Bear sat down at the edge of the river and folded the map smaller.
On the page, a gap where the bridge should be, and a bear very small beside the water.
Hal looks at the picture of the bridge. The pen is still in his hand.
Hal: Why doesn't the bear ask the rabbit about the bridge?
For a moment neither of you speaks.
Hal turns back, without being asked, to the picture of the two bowls. He looks at it for a while.
Hal: I put out two cups every morning. Habit.
A beat.
Hal: I know she isn't coming down.
Hal studies the picture of the bridge. He seems about to say something, and does not.
Hal: Well. Back to the bridge.
That is as far as this version of the act goes.
That is as far as this version of the act goes.
